title: Compilers, Build Tools and Static Analysis
objectives: Select compiler flags for debug vs release builds and explain what each controls
Describe the role of Ninja and CMake in a build pipeline and how incremental builds work
Run clang-tidy with targeted checks and clang-format, and explain warnings-as-errors policy
Diagnose a common warning (signed/unsigned comparison) and fix it at the source
motivation: A new hire builds the pricing library with plain `g++ main.cpp`, runs it, and ships numbers that are wrong, because their signed loop variable compared against `vector.size()` never terminated the intended way, a warning that `-Wall -Werror` would have rejected at compile time. Tooling is not bureaucracy: flags, fast incremental builds and static analysis are the difference between bugs caught in seconds and bugs caught in production.

blocks.text: Compiler flags: two builds, two jobs

blocks.md: C++ has no single 'the' build, you maintain at least two. The **debug build** compiles fast, keeps every diagnostic on, and is shaped for humans: optimisation off (`-O0`) so the debugger's line-by-line view matches the source, debug symbols (`-g`) so GDB and perf can name things. The **release build** is shaped for the machine: `-O2`/`-O3` optimisation, `-DNDEBUG` to compile out asserts, and `-g` kept anyway so profilers still map addresses to lines, symbols cost disk, not runtime. Warnings come from `-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic` (not literally 'all', but the high-signal set), and `-Werror` promotes any warning to a build failure so warnings cannot accumulate into wallpaper.

blocks.code:
# Debug build: fast compile, full checks, debuggable
g++ -std=c++20 -O0 -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror \
    -fsanitize=address,undefined src/*.cpp -o app_debug

# Release build: aggressive optimisation, symbols kept for profiling
g++ -std=c++20 -O3 -g -march=native -DNDEBUG src/*.cpp -o app_release

# -std=c++20 pins the language version (code must not depend on the
# compiler's default). -march=native targets this CPU's ISA (SIMD lesson).
# -DNDEBUG disables assert() in release - assertions are for debug runs.
blocks.caption: Two commands, two contracts: debug finds bugs, release wins benchmarks.

rows: O0 for debuggability, O2/O3 for speed; never compare timings across levels
Lets GDB/perf show source lines; harmless at runtime
Catches signed/unsigned, unused values, shadowing, non-standard code
Keeps warnings from being ignored; standard in CI
Release builds should not pay for debug assertions
Enables AVX2/AVX-512 codegen for this machine (portability trade-off)

blocks.text: CMake and Ninja: builds that scale

blocks.md: Typing compiler commands stops scaling at a handful of files. **CMake** describes the project (targets, dependencies, options) and *generates* build files for a chosen backend; **Ninja** is the backend built for speed, it evaluates a dependency graph and executes the minimum recompilation in parallel, one compiler process per core. Change one `.cpp` and Ninja rebuilds that file plus whatever links it; change a header and everything that includes it rebuilds. Compile-time is a feedback loop for correctness work like the warning discipline above, so fast incremental builds change behaviour, not just wall-clock.

blocks.code:
cmake -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release   # configure: generate build.ninja
cmake --build build                                   # or: ninja -C build
ninja -C build                                        # incremental: rebuilds only what changed
# Release/Debug build types set the flag sets shown above per configuration.
blocks.caption: CMake generates; Ninja executes. The two-file change you made costs seconds, not minutes.

blocks.text: Static analysis: the reviewer that never gets tired

blocks.md: Compiler warnings catch what the compiler notices; dedicated static analysers go further. **clang-tidy** runs named checks over your code with full AST knowledge: `bugprone-*` (suspicious constructs), `performance-*` (inefficient patterns), `modernize-*` (pre-C++11 idioms to update), `clang-analyzer-*` (path-sensitive bug finding). **clang-format** ends style debates: a `.clang-format` file specifies formatting, and `clang-format -i` rewrites files to match, diffs stop containing whitespace noise. The pipeline standard: format check + `clang-tidy` + `-Werror` on every commit.

blocks.code:
clang-tidy src/pricer.cpp -p build/ \
    -checks='-*,bugprone-*,performance-*,modernize-*'   # -p: use compile_commands.json

clang-format -i src/pricer.cpp                          # rewrite in place to project style

# .clang-format (project root):
#   BasedOnStyle: Google
#   IndentWidth: 4
#   ColumnLimit: 100
#   DerivePointerAlignment: false
blocks.caption: Tidy finds logic-shape bugs; format enforces one style; both run mechanically.

blocks.md: C++ tooling is a pipeline you must be able to reason about end-to-end, because the compiler is where half your performance comes from and all of your correctness guarantees originate. The pipeline: preprocessor → compiler proper (optimisation levels decide how hard it works) → linker (where the One-Definition Rule and visibility questions land) → and alongside it, the analysers: sanitisers and static analysis, which catch bug classes the compiler silently tolerates.

rows: what does style + bugs look like?
how hard does the compiler try?

blocks.code:
# The debugging loop that finds real bugs fast:
g++ -std=c++20 -g -O1 -fsanitize=address,undefined -o pricer_asan pricer.cpp
./pricer_asan input.csv          # ASan prints the exact allocation stack of any OOB

# Then optimise and benchmark the FIXED code:
g++ -std=c++20 -O2 -march=native -o pricer pricer.cpp
perf stat -e task-clock,cache-misses ./pricer input.csv
blocks.caption: Sanitise first, optimise second. Optimising buggy code optimises the bug.

steps.note: formatting is not taste, it is policy: one file, one verdict

out: warning: loop variable copied on each iteration [performance-for-range-copy]
warning: narrowing conversion from double to float [bugprone-narrowing]
steps.note: static analysis reads the code you wrote against the code you meant
every tool downstream reads one index: clangd, tidy, coverage all speak it

blocks.caption: Tools are compilers that output opinions instead of objects. The index file they share is what makes a codebase navigable.

blocks.md: The ordering discipline matters more than any individual flag. Debug with sanitisers at `-O1` (fast enough to run, faithful enough to diagnose). Benchmark only at `-O2`/`-O3` with `-march=native` on the target hardware, after the sanitisers are clean, because UB that "works" at `-O0` becomes the miscompiled loop you ship at `-O2`. And treat warnings as errors from day one (`-Werror`): a warning you learn to scroll past is a bug you have scheduled for later.

blocks.title: "It works at -O0" is a UB confession
blocks.md: The single most diagnostic sentence in C++ debugging. Optimisation exposes undefined behaviour, the compiler assumes UB never happens and optimises accordingly (dead-code elimination, reordering, vectorisation). If behaviour changes between -O0 and -O2, you do not have a compiler bug; you have UB, and the sanitisers will name it.

blocks.title: Worked diagnosis: the signed/unsigned loop
items: Code: `for (int i = 0; i < v.size(); ++i) { ... }` where `v.size()` is `std::size_t` (unsigned 64-bit).
`-Wall -Wextra` emits: *comparison of integer expressions of different signedness*.

Why it is a real bug class: when `i` is compared to an unsigned value it is converted to unsigned; if `v` is empty, `v.size()` is 0 and `0 - 1` in unsigned arithmetic is $2^{64} - 1$ - loops like `while (i <= v.size() - 1)` on empty vectors wrap and run off the end.
Fixes: use `std::size_t i`, or better `for (const auto& x : v)`, or `std::ssize(v)` (C++20) to keep signedness consistent.
With `-Werror` this never reaches review: the build fails and the author fixes it in seconds.

blocks.title: Do not silence: understand
blocks.md: The lazy fix for any warning is a cast or deleting the flag. Each warning suppresses a class of future bug detection too. The professional move: understand *why* the tool fired, fix the code, and only with a written justification (and a code comment or targeted check-disable) bypass anything.

guidedExercise.prompt: A teammate's build shows: `warning: comparison of integer expressions of different signedness: 'int' and 'std::vector<Quote>::size_type' {aka 'unsigned long'}` at `for (int i = 0; i < quotes.size() - 1; ++i)`. Explain the danger when `quotes` is empty, and give two idiomatic fixes.
hints: What is the type of `quotes.size() - 1` when size() returns 0?
Range-for removes the index entirely; C++20 std::ssize keeps indices but fixes signedness.
guidedExercise.solution: `quotes.size()` is unsigned, so `size() - 1` with `size() == 0` wraps to $2^{64}-1$ (the largest unsigned long); the comparison converts `i` to unsigned, and the loop believes there are ~$1.8 \times 10^{19}$ elements, it reads wildly out of bounds instead of skipping the loop. Fixes: (1) `for (std::size_t i = 0; i + 1 < quotes.size(); ++i)` - the `i + 1 <` form avoids the wrap because `i + 1` cannot underflow; (2) `for (const auto& q : quotes)` when the index is not needed, or `for (int i = 0; i < std::ssize(quotes) - 1; ++i)` in C++20 (signed `ssize`). With -Werror the original never compiles.

independentExercise.prompt: Set up the build/check pipeline for a two-file project `pricer.cpp` and `book.cpp` (headers included). Write: (a) the CMake configure line choosing Ninja and the Release configuration; (b) the incremental build command after editing only `book.cpp`; (c) the clang-tidy command checking `bugprone-*`, `performance-*` and `modernize-*` with the compile database from the build directory; (d) the clang-format command to fix formatting across both files, and one sentence on why the format step belongs before code review rather than during it.
hints: cmake -B <dir> -G <generator> -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=<type>; building via cmake --build or ninja -C.
clang-tidy needs -p pointing at the directory with compile_commands.json (generate with CMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS).
independentExercise.solution: (a) `cmake -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON`. (b) `ninja -C build` (or `cmake --build build`). Ninja's dependency graph rebuilds only `book.o` and relinks. (c) `clang-tidy src/book.cpp src/pricer.cpp -p build/ -checks='-*,bugprone-*,performance-*,modernize-*'`. (d) `clang-format -i src/pricer.cpp src/book.cpp`; format before review so reviewers see semantic diffs only, whitespace churn in review wastes attention and hides real changes.

commonMistakes: Building release code without -g and then being unable to profile or get a readable crash backtrace.
Treating -Wall as 'all warnings' and skipping -Wextra -Wpedantic; the high-value signed/unsigned and shadowing warnings live in -Wextra.
Letting warnings accumulate (no -Werror) until the real signal drowns in wallpaper.
Committing formatting churn mixed with logic changes because clang-format was never run.
Using -march=native for binaries that must run on other machines, the release artefact then crashes with SIGILL on older CPUs.
realWorldApplication: Every production C++ shop standardises on CMake+Ninja (or Bazel), warnings-as-errors in CI, clang-format enforced by a commit hook, and clang-tidy on changed lines, the pipeline is the codebase's immune system.
quantFinanceApplication: Trading-firm codebases gate every commit on -Werror builds and sanitiser jobs so a signedness wrap in a position loop or a stray allocation in the hot path is caught before it can reach a live order stream.
summary: Two builds by contract: -O0 -g with warnings+sanitisers for debugging; -O3 -DNDEBUG -g -march=native for performance.
-Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror converts the high-signal warning set into build failures, keeping signal high.
CMake generates the dependency graph, Ninja executes the minimum rebuild in parallel, fast feedback enables discipline.
clang-tidy (bugprone/performance/modernize checks) and clang-format (one style, zero whitespace debates) run mechanically on every change.
Signed/unsigned comparison is the canonical caught-by-tooling bug: unsigned wraparound on empty containers; fix with size_t/range-for/std::ssize.

options: Turns compiler warnings into errors, failing the build
Suppresses warnings so output stays clean
Errors only on warnings involving UB
quiz.explanation: -Werror changes the policy: any warning fails the build, which is why CI uses it, warnings cannot accumulate into ignored wallpaper.

quiz.prompt: Why do production release builds typically keep `-g` even though nothing is debugged at build time?
options: Symbols let profilers, core dumps and crash reports map addresses to source lines, at no runtime cost
Without -g the linker strips the binary
quiz.explanation: Debug symbols live in a table, not in the hot path: profiling, post-mortem debugging and symbolication all need them. (They do enlarge the binary, some shops ship them separately.)

quiz.prompt: In one sentence each: what do CMake and Ninja each contribute to a build pipeline?
quiz.modelAnswer: CMake describes targets/dependencies and generates build files; Ninja executes the dependency graph, rebuilding only what changed in parallel.
quiz.explanation: CMake is the project description/generator (build.ninja via -G Ninja); Ninja is the fast parallel executor of the minimal incremental rebuild.

quiz.prompt: `for (int i = 0; i < v.size() - 1; ++i)` with `v.size() == 0`. What happens at the first comparison and why?
options: The loop body never runs because size(), 1 is -1
`size() - 1` wraps to a huge unsigned value, the comparison converts i to unsigned, and the loop runs far out of bounds
The compiler rejects it at -O2 only
quiz.explanation: size_t arithmetic: 0, 1 = 2^64, 1. The signed int i is converted to unsigned for the comparison, so the loop sees an enormous bound. This is exactly what -Wall's sign-compare warning flags.

quiz.prompt: Which clang-tidy check family targets suspicious constructs likely to be bugs (rather than style or modernisation)?
quiz.explanation: bugprone-* covers suspicious constructs; performance-* inefficiency; modernize-* legacy idioms; readability-* style. A typical run enables bugprone, performance and modernize together.

quiz.prompt: You run: `ninja -C build` after editing exactly one .cpp file (no headers changed) in a 3-file project. Ninja prints one compile line and one link line. How many translation units are recompiled?
quiz.code:
# build.ninja tracks dependencies from compile_commands/depfiles
# project: pricer.cpp, book.cpp, main.cpp  -> app
# you edited book.cpp only
$ ninja -C build
quiz.explanation: Ninja's dependency graph recompiles only book.cpp (one translation unit) and then relinks the app, that minimum-rebuild property is the point of the tool.

flashcards.back: All compiler warnings are build errors. Rationale: warnings encode real bug classes (sign-compare, shadowing, unused values); failing the build keeps signal high.
Debug: -O0 -g -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -fsanitize=... . Release: -O3 -DNDEBUG -g -march=native. First finds bugs, second produces numbers.
CMake: describes targets, generates build files (build.ninja with -G Ninja). Ninja: executes the dependency graph with minimal, parallel, incremental rebuilds.
clang-tidy: AST-based static analysis with named check families (bugprone/performance/modernize). clang-format: mechanical formatting from .clang-format so style is never discussed in review.
